text.p: Kuwait swore in a new 14-man cabinet on Wednesday that will be concerned with former occupier Iraq and raising revenue by exporting more refined products.

The 14-man cabinet, formed on Tuesday night and headed by Crown Prince Sheikh Saad al-Abdulla al-Sabah, took the oath of office on Wednesday before holding its first meeting under Kuwait Emir Sheikh Jaber al-Ahmad al-Sabah.

Oil Minister Isa al-Mazeedi's task of running the country's foreign currency earner has been made easier by soaring world oil prices. The U.S.-educated minister also heads the state's oil conglomerate Kuwait Petroleum Corporation.
Defence Minister Sheikh Salem Sabah al-Salem al-Sabah, 59, will oversee a $11.7 billion 1992-2004 plan to rebuild the military after the disaster of the 1990 Iraqi invasion.

The defence minister studied law in Britain where he later was ambassador. He helped found Kuwait's foreign ministry and also served as ambassador to Washington. He first headed the defence ministry in 1978.
The cabinet, which includes four elected MPS, was formed after last week's parliament election that were dominated with debates on perceived Iraqi threats.

The new parliament, which convenes on October 20 and will last into the next century, is predicted to be less confrontational than the last opposition-dominated one. Many pro-government MPs won seats.

Kuwait's first parliament after the 1991 Gulf War probed alleged official corruption and misuse of public funds. It also questioned arms deals with Western allies and the state's handling of events prior to Iraq's occupation.

Sheikh Sabah al-Ahmad al-Sabah, one of the world's longest serving foreign ministers, kept his post and the title of first deputy prime minister. He had been foreign minister for 28 years when he was not included in the 1991 cabinet.
Besides Sheikh Saad, 66, who has been prime minister since 1978, the new cabinet has four other members of the al-Sabah family that has ruled Kuwait since 1752.

The governor of the oil city of al-Ahmadi, Sheikh Mohammad Khaled al-Sabah, was named interior minister while Sheikh Saud Nasser al-Sabah, ambassador to Washington during the Gulf crisis, kept the information ministry. He is also acting health minister.
Nasser Abdulla al-Rodhan will continue as finance minister, running the tiny country's economy and overseeing a foreign investment portfolio valued at about $35 billion.

The outgoing parliament approved a 1996/97 state budget of $14 billion with a forecast deficit of $4 billion. Oil revenue was calculated at a conservative weighted average price of $13 a barrel but world prices have since risen, exceeding $25 a barrel for Brent.
Kuwait has a daily Organisation of Petroleum Exporting Countries (OPEC) quota of two million barrels and is working to raise exports of higher-value products.
